parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 6. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a woman asking a friend about a pottery class that he goes to. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 6. Amy: Hi, Rob. Have you got a minute? Jess told me you've started going to a pottery class. Rob: Yes, I have, and I'm really enjoying it. Are you thinking of joining? I've been going for about six weeks now. Amy: I might be. I've always wanted to try it. Who teaches it? Rob: Her name's Sarah Kenyon. She's a professional potter, and she sells her work at craft fairs all over the region. Amy: Kenyon. How do you spell that? Rob: K, E, N, Y, O, N. Amy: Thanks. And what level is it? I've never touched clay in my life. Rob: Don't worry. The poster says it's for mixed abilities, but when I spoke to Sarah, she said it's really aimed at beginners. Most of us had never done it before. Amy: That's a relief. Where is it held? Rob: When I started, it was in Sarah's own studio, which is actually her garage. But there wasn't enough room, so now we meet in the library, in a big room in the basement. Amy: The library? Which one? The one on Market Street? Rob: No, that's the old one. The new one's just round the corner, on Bridge Street, opposite the bus station. Amy: Oh yes, I know it. And when's the class? Rob: It's on Tuesday evenings. It used to start at seven, but a yoga group uses the room before us, and they asked for more time, so now it starts at seven thirty. Amy: That's actually better for me. And how much does it cost? Rob: It's ninety-five pounds for a ten-week term. That includes all the clay and the glazes. There's a small extra charge if you want to make something really big, but most people don't bother. Amy: That seems reasonable. Do I need to bring anything? Rob: Just an old shirt or an apron, and a towel. Oh, and short fingernails! Amy: Ha! OK. And how many people are in the group? Rob: Usually about ten. Sarah doesn't want more than twelve, so that everyone gets some individual help. It's a really friendly group, too. We often go for a coffee together afterwards. Amy: That sounds lovely. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10. Amy: So what actually happens in a class? Rob: Well, it lasts two hours altogether. We always start by preparing the clay. We spend about ten minutes kneading it, a bit like making bread. That gets rid of any air bubbles, which is important, because if there's air trapped inside, a piece can crack when it's heated. Amy: Really? I'd never have guessed that. Rob: Then there's about forty minutes of hand-building. That means making things without the wheel. Sometimes we roll the clay into long coils and build them up into a pot, and sometimes we cut it into flat slabs and join them together to make boxes or tiles. Amy: That sounds fun. Rob: It is. After that there's a short break, and then forty minutes on the wheel. That's the hardest part. Sarah always gives a demonstration first, so we can see exactly what to do, and then she goes round helping everyone. She doesn't give out any written instructions, so you have to watch really carefully. Amy: I'm sure I'll be terrible at that. Rob: Everyone is at first. My first few pots all collapsed. Then, for the last part of the lesson, there's about twenty minutes of glazing, when we paint the pieces we made the week before. Sarah puts them in the kiln after the class, and they're fired during the following week, so you have to be patient. Amy: And is there time to clear up at the end? Rob: Yes, the last ten minutes. Everyone helps to wash the tools and wipe down the tables. Amy: And do you get to keep the things you make? Rob: Yes, once they've been fired, you can take them home. My kitchen is full of rather strange-looking bowls now, but I'm very proud of them. Amy: Well, it sounds great. I'll give Sarah a ring this week. Rob: Brilliant. See you there, I hope. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a man called Ian talking on a local radio programme about his work as a mountain rescue volunteer. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Ian: Thanks for inviting me onto the programme. I never really expected to become a mountain rescue volunteer. Ten years ago, I was working as an accountant in Leeds. The job itself was fine, and the hours weren't too bad, but I'd been climbing since I was a teenager, and I realised I wanted to live somewhere I could get out onto the hills every weekend. So I moved up here to the Lake District, and not long afterwards, I saw that the local rescue team was looking for volunteers. Ian: Our team is based in a new building just outside the town. People often assume it was paid for by the national park or by a government grant, but in fact the money came from a local farmer, who left a large sum to the team in her will. Like all mountain rescue teams in this country, we're a charity, so gifts like that make an enormous difference. Ian: Before I could join, I had to have a medical. They checked my eyesight, which was fine, and my weight, which was fine too, back then! What concerned the doctor was an old knee injury from my football days. I had to see a physiotherapist and do some extra tests before they'd let me go out on rescues. Ian: When someone calls for help, the police contact us, and every volunteer gets a message on their phone. Most of us live within ten minutes of the base, and our aim is to have the first team leaving the base within twenty minutes of the call. The average for teams across the country is nearer thirty, so we're quite proud of that. Ian: Last year, I became a team leader, which means that on a callout I'm in charge of the people on the hill. The route we take is usually agreed with the police, and helicopters are requested by the coastguard, not by us. My responsibility is deciding whether it's safe for the team to carry on with a search, especially when the weather gets worse. Ian: Rescues aren't the only part of the job. A lot of the people we help are simply unprepared. They're wearing the wrong shoes, or they haven't checked the weather forecast. So I spend quite a lot of time going into schools and youth clubs to give talks on how to walk safely in the hills. Other members of the team run first aid courses for the public, and we have a retired mechanic who looks after our vehicles. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. Ian: The training never really stops. We practise navigation, rope work and casualty care out on the hills almost every week. The navigation training was quite demanding, actually, because you have to be able to find your way in thick fog without relying on GPS. The first aid part was hard work too, but I'd done a course before, so I didn't find it too challenging. Ian: What the training has done more than anything is make me calmer. When I first joined, my heart would be racing on every callout, but now I can stay focused even when things are going badly. Once a year, we also do a night exercise in the mountains in the middle of winter, where we practise how to survive if we're stuck out overnight in terrible weather. That's been invaluable. Ian: So why do I keep doing it? Well, people do sometimes write to thank us, which is lovely, but that's not really why I do it. For me, the best thing is the people in the team. We've been through some really tough nights together, and we're like a family now. And I have to say, I've never been fitter. I'm nearly fifty, and I'm in better shape than I was at thirty, which is a great feeling. Ian: We've recently started using a drone to search for missing walkers, which is fascinating, but I tend to leave that to the younger members. And the winter rescues are the part I enjoy least, to be honest. They mean long, cold nights on the hill. But I wouldn't give up this work for anything. So, if any of your listeners are interested in volunteering, please get in touch. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two students, Nadia and Sam, discussing a presentation they are preparing on recycling mobile phones. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Nadia: Hi, Sam. Did you get a chance to read the article I sent you about recycling mobile phones? Sam: Yes, I read it last night. Nadia: So, do you think it would work as a topic for our presentation? Sam: Well, to be honest, before I read it, I thought it might be too technical. I imagined it would be all about chemistry and circuit boards, and that the audience would be lost after five minutes. Nadia: But it isn't really like that, is it? Sam: No. There's a lot about people's behaviour, which is much easier to follow. I'm quite keen on it now. Nadia: I think our tutor will like it too, because it links to what we've been studying about the circular economy. Sam: True. And everyone in the audience will have a phone, so they'll all be able to relate to it. Nadia: Good. One thing that struck me was how often people change their phones. Sam: Every two or three years, it said. That seems about right to me. Nadia: Me too. But I think the phone companies are to blame for that. They bring out a new model every year and make people feel that their old phone is out of date. Sam: I don't agree. I think people choose to upgrade because they want better cameras and so on. Nobody forces them to do it. Nadia: Well, we'll have to agree to differ on that one. Do you still have any old phones? Sam: No, I always trade mine in. What about you? Nadia: I've got three in a drawer at home. I don't really need them as spares or anything, and I know where the recycling point is. The trouble is, they've all got photos on them that I've never backed up, and I'm scared of losing them. Sam: You should sort that out! Anyway, what I found most surprising in the article was the gold. I knew phones contained metals like copper, but I had no idea that a tonne of old phones contains far more gold than a tonne of the rock that gold is normally mined from. Nadia: Yes, that amazed me too. I knew huge numbers of phones are sold every year, but I'd never thought about what's inside them. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Nadia: The article included an interview with the manager of a company that refurbishes old phones. He described some phones that they couldn't use. Sam: Right, let's go through them. First there was the latest model, which must have cost a fortune. Nadia: Yes. It looked perfect, but when they opened it up, they found that someone had replaced the screen with a cheap copy that wasn't made by the manufacturer. They can't sell phones with parts like that. Sam: Then there was the gold-coloured phone. Nadia: That was in great condition, with hardly a scratch on it. But the owner hadn't signed out of their account before handing it in, so it was still locked, and the company had no way of contacting them. Sam: What about the child's phone, the one with the cartoon stickers? Nadia: Oh, yes. Surprisingly, the screen was fine, and it hadn't been dropped in water or anything. But the battery had swollen so much that the back of the phone had started to come away. That's actually quite dangerous. Sam: And the business phone? Nadia: It was only three years old, so updates weren't a problem. But it had a crack right across the screen, and the touchscreen didn't respond at all. Replacing it would have cost more than the phone was worth. Sam: Did you read about the trade-in scheme that one of the big shops tried? They offered customers money off a new phone if they handed in their old one. And they advertised it everywhere. Nadia: Yes, but it didn't really work, did it? Sam: No. I assumed it was because the prices they offered were too low. Nadia: That's what I thought too. But the survey they did afterwards found that the main reason was that customers were worried their personal data wouldn't be completely erased. Sam: That makes sense. I'd be worried about that too. So, how should we approach the presentation? We don't want to overload people with statistics. Nadia: No. And most presentations on this subject just tell people how to recycle more. I think it would be more interesting to focus on what actually happens to a phone after you hand it in: where it goes, and who deals with it. Sam: Yes, that's a much fresher angle. Let's do that. Nadia: Shall we split the research? You could look into the refurbishing companies, and I'll find out about the plants where the metals are recovered. Sam: Good idea. Let's meet again on Friday and see what we've got. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a biology student giving a presentation about an animal called the axolotl. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: For my project on amphibians, I chose to study the axolotl, a type of salamander that has become quite popular on the internet in recent years, thanks to its unusual, smiling face. The name comes from the language of the Aztecs, and it's usually linked to Xolotl, an Aztec god associated with fire and lightning, who, according to legend, turned himself into an axolotl to escape death. I first became interested in them after seeing one at a friend's house, where it lived in a large tank in the living room. Student: In the wild, axolotls are found in only one place in the world: the network of canals and lakes at Xochimilco, on the southern edge of Mexico City. They can grow to around thirty centimetres in length, although most are smaller, and in captivity they can live for ten to fifteen years. Student: What makes the axolotl so unusual is that, unlike most amphibians, it never goes through metamorphosis. Frogs, for example, begin life as tadpoles in the water and then develop into adults that can live on land. The axolotl, however, keeps its larval features throughout its life and spends its whole life in water. The most obvious of these features are the three pairs of feathery external gills that stick out from the sides of its head. But the gills aren't its only way of breathing. It also has simple lungs, and it can take in some oxygen through its skin. Student: In the wild, axolotls are usually dark brown or black, often with darker spots, which helps to camouflage them against the bottom of the canals. The pale pink ones that you often see in photographs are rare in the wild. They're mainly bred in laboratories and for the pet trade. Student: Axolotls are of great interest to scientists because of their remarkable ability to regenerate. If an axolotl loses a leg, it can grow a complete new one, with bones, muscles and nerves, within a few weeks. And it's not just legs. Axolotls can also regenerate parts of the heart, the spinal cord and even the brain. What's more, when humans heal, we usually form scars, but axolotls regrow tissue without forming any scars at all. Researchers hope that understanding how they do this could one day help doctors to treat serious injuries in humans. Remarkably, they seem to be able to do this again and again throughout their lives. Student: In terms of their diet, axolotls are carnivores. In the wild, they eat worms, insect larvae, water snails and small fish. They don't chew their food. Instead, when prey comes close, they open their mouths very suddenly and use suction to pull it in. Student: Finally, I'd like to talk about the axolotl's conservation status. Although axolotls are common in aquariums and laboratories around the world, in the wild they're critically endangered, and surveys suggest that their numbers in Xochimilco have fallen dramatically since the late nineteen nineties. There are several reasons for this. As Mexico City has grown, much of the axolotl's habitat has been drained or built on, and the water that remains is often polluted. Another major threat comes from fish such as carp and tilapia, which were introduced into the canals in the past to provide food for local people. These fish compete with axolotls for food, and they also eat axolotl eggs. Some scientists fear that there may soon be no axolotls left in the wild at all, which would be a strange situation for one of the most studied animals in the world. Student: Fortunately, conservationists are now working with local farmers who still grow crops on small artificial islands in the canals, using traditional methods. Together, they've created protected areas in some of the canals, where they place filters at the entrances to keep out the introduced fish and to clean the water. Early results suggest that axolotls are returning to these areas. So, does anyone have any questions? That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a man called Ian talking on a local radio programme about his work as a mountain rescue volunteer. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Ian: Thanks for inviting me onto the programme. I never really expected to become a mountain rescue volunteer. Ten years ago, I was working as an accountant in Leeds. The job itself was fine, and the hours weren't too bad, but I'd been climbing since I was a teenager, and I realised I wanted to live somewhere I could get out onto the hills every weekend. So I moved up here to the Lake District, and not long afterwards, I saw that the local rescue team was looking for volunteers. Ian: Our team is based in a new building just outside the town. People often assume it was paid for by the national park or by a government grant, but in fact the money came from a local farmer, who left a large sum to the team in her will. Like all mountain rescue teams in this country, we're a charity, so gifts like that make an enormous difference. Ian: Before I could join, I had to have a medical. They checked my eyesight, which was fine, and my weight, which was fine too, back then! What concerned the doctor was an old knee injury from my football days. I had to see a physiotherapist and do some extra tests before they'd let me go out on rescues. Ian: When someone calls for help, the police contact us, and every volunteer gets a message on their phone. Most of us live within ten minutes of the base, and our aim is to have the first team leaving the base within twenty minutes of the call. The average for teams across the country is nearer thirty, so we're quite proud of that. Ian: Last year, I became a team leader, which means that on a callout I'm in charge of the people on the hill. The route we take is usually agreed with the police, and helicopters are requested by the coastguard, not by us. My responsibility is deciding whether it's safe for the team to carry on with a search, especially when the weather gets worse. Ian: Rescues aren't the only part of the job. A lot of the people we help are simply unprepared. They're wearing the wrong shoes, or they haven't checked the weather forecast. So I spend quite a lot of time going into schools and youth clubs to give talks on how to walk safely in the hills. Other members of the team run first aid courses for the public, and we have a retired mechanic who looks after our vehicles. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. Ian: The training never really stops. We practise navigation, rope work and casualty care out on the hills almost every week. The navigation training was quite demanding, actually, because you have to be able to find your way in thick fog without relying on GPS. The first aid part was hard work too, but I'd done a course before, so I didn't find it too challenging. Ian: What the training has done more than anything is make me calmer. When I first joined, my heart would be racing on every callout, but now I can stay focused even when things are going badly. Once a year, we also do a night exercise in the mountains in the middle of winter, where we practise how to survive if we're stuck out overnight in terrible weather. That's been invaluable. Ian: So why do I keep doing it? Well, people do sometimes write to thank us, which is lovely, but that's not really why I do it. For me, the best thing is the people in the team. We've been through some really tough nights together, and we're like a family now. And I have to say, I've never been fitter. I'm nearly fifty, and I'm in better shape than I was at thirty, which is a great feeling. Ian: We've recently started using a drone to search for missing walkers, which is fascinating, but I tend to leave that to the younger members. And the winter rescues are the part I enjoy least, to be honest. They mean long, cold nights on the hill. But I wouldn't give up this work for anything. So, if any of your listeners are interested in volunteering, please get in touch. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two students, Nadia and Sam, discussing a presentation they are preparing on recycling mobile phones. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Nadia: Hi, Sam. Did you get a chance to read the article I sent you about recycling mobile phones? Sam: Yes, I read it last night. Nadia: So, do you think it would work as a topic for our presentation? Sam: Well, to be honest, before I read it, I thought it might be too technical. I imagined it would be all about chemistry and circuit boards, and that the audience would be lost after five minutes. Nadia: But it isn't really like that, is it? Sam: No. There's a lot about people's behaviour, which is much easier to follow. I'm quite keen on it now. Nadia: I think our tutor will like it too, because it links to what we've been studying about the circular economy. Sam: True. And everyone in the audience will have a phone, so they'll all be able to relate to it. Nadia: Good. One thing that struck me was how often people change their phones. Sam: Every two or three years, it said. That seems about right to me. Nadia: Me too. But I think the phone companies are to blame for that. They bring out a new model every year and make people feel that their old phone is out of date. Sam: I don't agree. I think people choose to upgrade because they want better cameras and so on. Nobody forces them to do it. Nadia: Well, we'll have to agree to differ on that one. Do you still have any old phones? Sam: No, I always trade mine in. What about you? Nadia: I've got three in a drawer at home. I don't really need them as spares or anything, and I know where the recycling point is. The trouble is, they've all got photos on them that I've never backed up, and I'm scared of losing them. Sam: You should sort that out! Anyway, what I found most surprising in the article was the gold. I knew phones contained metals like copper, but I had no idea that a tonne of old phones contains far more gold than a tonne of the rock that gold is normally mined from. Nadia: Yes, that amazed me too. I knew huge numbers of phones are sold every year, but I'd never thought about what's inside them. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Nadia: The article included an interview with the manager of a company that refurbishes old phones. He described some phones that they couldn't use. Sam: Right, let's go through them. First there was the latest model, which must have cost a fortune. Nadia: Yes. It looked perfect, but when they opened it up, they found that someone had replaced the screen with a cheap copy that wasn't made by the manufacturer. They can't sell phones with parts like that. Sam: Then there was the gold-coloured phone. Nadia: That was in great condition, with hardly a scratch on it. But the owner hadn't signed out of their account before handing it in, so it was still locked, and the company had no way of contacting them. Sam: What about the child's phone, the one with the cartoon stickers? Nadia: Oh, yes. Surprisingly, the screen was fine, and it hadn't been dropped in water or anything. But the battery had swollen so much that the back of the phone had started to come away. That's actually quite dangerous. Sam: And the business phone? Nadia: It was only three years old, so updates weren't a problem. But it had a crack right across the screen, and the touchscreen didn't respond at all. Replacing it would have cost more than the phone was worth. Sam: Did you read about the trade-in scheme that one of the big shops tried? They offered customers money off a new phone if they handed in their old one. And they advertised it everywhere. Nadia: Yes, but it didn't really work, did it? Sam: No. I assumed it was because the prices they offered were too low. Nadia: That's what I thought too. But the survey they did afterwards found that the main reason was that customers were worried their personal data wouldn't be completely erased. Sam: That makes sense. I'd be worried about that too. So, how should we approach the presentation? We don't want to overload people with statistics. Nadia: No. And most presentations on this subject just tell people how to recycle more. I think it would be more interesting to focus on what actually happens to a phone after you hand it in: where it goes, and who deals with it. Sam: Yes, that's a much fresher angle. Let's do that. Nadia: Shall we split the research? You could look into the refurbishing companies, and I'll find out about the plants where the metals are recovered. Sam: Good idea. Let's meet again on Friday and see what we've got. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a biology student giving a presentation about an animal called the axolotl. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: For my project on amphibians, I chose to study the axolotl, a type of salamander that has become quite popular on the internet in recent years, thanks to its unusual, smiling face. The name comes from the language of the Aztecs, and it's usually linked to Xolotl, an Aztec god associated with fire and lightning, who, according to legend, turned himself into an axolotl to escape death. I first became interested in them after seeing one at a friend's house, where it lived in a large tank in the living room. Student: In the wild, axolotls are found in only one place in the world: the network of canals and lakes at Xochimilco, on the southern edge of Mexico City. They can grow to around thirty centimetres in length, although most are smaller, and in captivity they can live for ten to fifteen years. Student: What makes the axolotl so unusual is that, unlike most amphibians, it never goes through metamorphosis. Frogs, for example, begin life as tadpoles in the water and then develop into adults that can live on land. The axolotl, however, keeps its larval features throughout its life and spends its whole life in water. The most obvious of these features are the three pairs of feathery external gills that stick out from the sides of its head. But the gills aren't its only way of breathing. It also has simple lungs, and it can take in some oxygen through its skin. Student: In the wild, axolotls are usually dark brown or black, often with darker spots, which helps to camouflage them against the bottom of the canals. The pale pink ones that you often see in photographs are rare in the wild. They're mainly bred in laboratories and for the pet trade. Student: Axolotls are of great interest to scientists because of their remarkable ability to regenerate. If an axolotl loses a leg, it can grow a complete new one, with bones, muscles and nerves, within a few weeks. And it's not just legs. Axolotls can also regenerate parts of the heart, the spinal cord and even the brain. What's more, when humans heal, we usually form scars, but axolotls regrow tissue without forming any scars at all. Researchers hope that understanding how they do this could one day help doctors to treat serious injuries in humans. Remarkably, they seem to be able to do this again and again throughout their lives. Student: In terms of their diet, axolotls are carnivores. In the wild, they eat worms, insect larvae, water snails and small fish. They don't chew their food. Instead, when prey comes close, they open their mouths very suddenly and use suction to pull it in. Student: Finally, I'd like to talk about the axolotl's conservation status. Although axolotls are common in aquariums and laboratories around the world, in the wild they're critically endangered, and surveys suggest that their numbers in Xochimilco have fallen dramatically since the late nineteen nineties. There are several reasons for this. As Mexico City has grown, much of the axolotl's habitat has been drained or built on, and the water that remains is often polluted. Another major threat comes from fish such as carp and tilapia, which were introduced into the canals in the past to provide food for local people. These fish compete with axolotls for food, and they also eat axolotl eggs. Some scientists fear that there may soon be no axolotls left in the wild at all, which would be a strange situation for one of the most studied animals in the world. Student: Fortunately, conservationists are now working with local farmers who still grow crops on small artificial islands in the canals, using traditional methods. Together, they've created protected areas in some of the canals, where they place filters at the entrances to keep out the introduced fish and to clean the water. Early results suggest that axolotls are returning to these areas. So, does anyone have any questions? That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
